parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A woman phones a removal company to arrange moving house.
script: Good morning, Harbourline Removals, Callum speaking. How can I help you?
Oh, good morning. I'm hoping to get a quote for moving house next month. A friend of mine used you last year and she recommended you.
That's kind of her. Of course, I can take a few details now and then we can talk about the van and the price. Could I start with your surname?
Nearly. It's T-E-N-N-A-N-T. Two Ns in the middle.
Thank you. And a contact number, please?
07811 462 905. Lovely. And where will you be moving from?
It's 27 Marlow Road, in Highfield. That's M-A-R-L-O-W.
Got it. And the new address?
It's number 9, Quarry Lane, that's Q-U-A-R-R-Y, in Stonebridge. It's about twenty miles from here, so quite a drive.
That's no problem at all. Now, when were you thinking of moving?
I was hoping for Saturday the 11th of October, if you have a van free.
Hmm, let me have a look. Oh, I'm afraid the 11th is fully booked. We do have the 18th, which is also a Saturday, or the Monday after that.
The 18th would be fine, actually. I don't get the keys until the Friday before, so that gives me a bit more time to pack.
Good, I'll put you down for the 18th. We'd normally start at 8, but that crew is already on another job in the morning, so would 8.30 suit you?
8.30 is perfect. It means I can have breakfast first.
Great. And roughly how many boxes do you think you'll have? We bring the boxes for you, so we need to know how many.
Well, I've counted about 30 so far, but that's before I start on the kitchen and the garage. I suppose 40 is more realistic.
Let's say 40, then. Most people end up with more than they expect, so that's sensible. Are there any large or unusual items we should know about? A piano, for example?
No piano, thank goodness. But there's a grandfather clock that belonged to my father. It's rather delicate, and I'd hate it to be damaged.
We'll wrap that separately and send two people to carry it. What about big appliances, like a washing machine?
No, the washing machine is built in, so that stays with the house.

Fine. Now, we do offer insurance for the move. The basic cover is 18 pounds, but that only pays out up to 2,000 pounds in total, which probably isn't enough with a clock like yours. The full cover costs 24 pounds 50.
Then I'll take the full cover, please. I'd rather be safe.

Very wise. Now, to confirm the booking we ask for a deposit. For a three-bedroom house like yours, our medium van is ideal, and the deposit on that is 50 pounds. The large lorry would be 100 pounds, but you shouldn't need it.
The medium one sounds right. Can I pay the deposit by card over the phone?
Certainly. I'll transfer you to our accounts team in a moment. Before I do, is there anything else I can help with? Parking, for instance? Some streets are quite narrow.
Quarry Lane is wide enough, I think, but the neighbour at Marlow Road has a van of his own, so I'll ask him to move it that morning.
Good idea. We'll also email you a checklist with some packing tips, and our team leader will phone you the evening before to confirm the time.
That's very helpful. Thank you so much, Callum.
You're welcome, Mrs Tennant. I'll put you through to accounts now.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A guide gives an introductory talk at a maritime museum.
script: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Tidewater Maritime Museum. My name's Ross, and I'll be your guide for the next hour or so. Before we set off, I'd like to say a few words about the building itself, and about how the morning will work.

Many visitors assume that this building was once the customs house, mostly because of the little clock tower on the front. In fact, it was built in 1884 as a rope works. Ships needed hundreds of metres of rope, and this long, narrow ground floor was ideal for twisting it. The rope works closed in the 1960s, and the building stood empty for almost thirty years before it became the museum you see today.

Now, a few practical points. Photography is very welcome in every gallery. I know that some museums ban it altogether, but we don't. All I ask is that you switch off your flash, because it can fade the old paintings and charts.
If you're carrying bags or large coats, there are lockers beside the ticket desk. You'll need a one pound coin to lock one, but don't worry, the coin comes back to you when you return the key.

For anyone with children, I should mention that we do have costumes for dressing up as sailors, but they're only out during the school holidays, so not today, I'm afraid. What we do have all year round is a trail sheet from the desk. The children follow the clues from gallery to gallery, and anyone who finishes the trail is given a badge. It keeps them busy, and it keeps the adults free to read the labels.

You'll also notice that the Steam Gallery on the first floor has a sign saying it's closed for maintenance. Strictly speaking, that isn't quite true. The roof is perfectly sound. We're actually installing a brand new display about the first steam-powered ferries, which opens in the spring, so do come back and see it.

Let me tell you where everything is, because the layout is a little confusing. Most guidebooks still say that our café is on the ground floor, but it moved last year, and you'll now find it on the roof terrace. It's worth the climb, as you can drink your coffee looking out over the whole harbour.

Our collection of model ships is on the mezzanine, just up those stairs behind me. There are more than two hundred models, some of them made by sailors on long voyages, and one made entirely from matchsticks.

Down in the cellar, you'll find the objects that divers have recovered from shipwrecks around this coast. There are anchors, bottles, plates, and even a captain's sea chest that was still locked when it was brought up. The cellar is cool, so you may want to keep your coat on.

Across the courtyard, in the annexe, there's a workshop where volunteers teach you how to tie traditional sailors' knots. You can drop in at any time on Saturdays and Sundays, and it's very popular with families.

And finally, on the second floor, there's a small cinema showing a fifteen-minute film about the harbour as it looked a hundred years ago. It's shown every half hour, and it uses real footage, so I'd recommend it if you want to understand what the workers on the docks were doing.

The ground floor, where we're standing now, has the ticket desk, the shop and the information point, so if you have any questions during your visit, please come and ask any of the staff in our blue jackets.

Right, if you'd all like to follow me, we'll begin in the entrance hall with a look at the figurehead from the ship Constance, which is one of the museum's most famous objects. Please stay together, and mind the step as we go through the door.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two students, Nadia and Dan, discuss a group presentation on recycling plastics.
script: Hi, Nadia. Thanks for coming. I really wanted to sort out our presentation on recycling plastics before the end of the week.
Sure, no problem. I've been thinking about it all weekend, actually. It's funny how we ended up with this topic.
Yes. I always thought it was because of that documentary Dr Carter showed us in the first week.

Was it? I remember it differently. I think it was the visit to the sorting plant that did it. Seeing all those bottles going along the conveyor belt, and then watching the workers pull out the wrong ones by hand.
Oh, you're right. The documentary was about oceans, wasn't it? The plant visit is what got us thinking about what really happens to plastic after it goes in the bin.
Exactly. So, where have you got to with the survey results?
Well, that's what's worrying me a bit. We only asked 40 residents. I'm afraid Dr Carter will say that's too few people to prove anything.

It is a small number, but this is a student project, not a government report. If we're honest about it and say so on the slide, I think it's fine. Markers like it when you show you understand the limits of your data.

Okay, that's a relief. I'll add a line about that. Now, can I ask your advice about something else? I've got to explain how the sorting process works, and I'm finding it really dry. What would you do?
Hmm. Words alone won't work, will they?
I thought about showing the video from the plant's website.

I watched that. It's twelve minutes long, and we've only got fifteen in total, so that's out. A flow diagram might work as a summary at the end, but to start with I'd bring in some actual samples, the different types of plastic, each with its number on the bottom, and pass them round. People remember what they can hold.

That's a good idea. I'll collect some from the recycling bins in the canteen. Oh, and there was something I wanted to check. The plant manager said one type of plastic caused the most trouble for the machines. Was it the thin bags?

The thin film does wrap round the machinery, yes, and that's a nuisance. But no, the biggest problem he mentioned was black plastic trays. The scanners can't detect the colour, so they just go straight to landfill.
Right, I'd forgotten that. I'll put it on a slide. Now, for the conclusion, I was going to recommend a deposit scheme, where you pay a bit extra on each bottle and get it back.

That's one option, certainly, but our survey showed that 60 per cent of people weren't sure which items go in the recycling bin. So I think the more direct recommendation is clearer labels on packaging.
Fair enough. Labels it is. I can mention the deposit scheme briefly as another idea.
Perfect. So, the structure. I'll open by holding up a sack of rubbish from the canteen, and ask the audience to guess how much of it could have been recycled.
Nice. Then it's my turn, and I'll cover the costs of recycling compared with sending waste to landfill.
Yes. Then I'll do the sorting process with the samples, and you finish with the survey and the conclusion. How long should we each have? Ten minutes?
That would be twenty in total, which is over the limit. We've got fifteen, so let's say 7 minutes each and leave one minute for questions.
That sounds right. And the slides are due on Friday, aren't they?
I thought so, but Dr Carter emailed to say it's been brought forward to Thursday, because he's away on Friday.
Oh, thanks for telling me. That means we need to practise soon. Shall we do a run-through on Wednesday afternoon? We could use the drama studio.
I think the studio is booked. I've reserved a group study room in the library for 4 o'clock instead, so we can practise there.
Brilliant. I'll bring the samples, and you bring the slides on a memory stick.
Deal. Thanks, Nadia, I feel much better about it now.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture on how sleep affects learning and memory.
script: Good afternoon, everyone. Today I'd like to talk about something that every one of you does, and that most of you probably don't do enough of: sleep. In particular, I want to look at what sleep does for learning and memory, and what that might mean for those of you who have exams coming up.

Let's begin with some background. A night's sleep isn't one continuous state. Instead, we pass through repeating cycles. You will often hear that a cycle lasts an hour, but the average is much closer to 90 minutes, and most adults go through four or five of them each night. Each cycle includes light sleep, deep sleep and REM sleep.

Now, to the link with memory. One of the best-known experiments was carried out by Dr Anneke Voss at a university in the Netherlands. Students were given a list of 100 pairs of words to learn in the evening. One group then went to bed as usual, while the other group stayed awake for the same length of time. When they were tested, the students who had slept recalled around 20 per cent more words. Some of you may remember a figure of 30 per cent from a newspaper, but that came from a different and much smaller study.

So why does sleep help? When you learn something new, the information is first held temporarily in a region of the brain called the hippocampus. During sleep, especially deep sleep, those memories are replayed and gradually moved to the cortex, the outer layer of the brain, where they're stored for the long term. This transfer seems to depend on short bursts of electrical activity known as sleep spindles. People who produce more spindles in the night tend to remember more of what they learned the day before.

Different stages seem to do different jobs. Deep sleep appears to be most important for facts, such as vocabulary and dates, while REM sleep is more closely linked with skills and creative problem solving.

This has some uncomfortable implications for teenagers. During adolescence the body clock shifts, so that young people naturally become sleepy about 2 hours later than children or adults. Early starts make them miss valuable sleep. A trial in twelve secondary schools moved the start of the day back by an hour. Results improved in several subjects, but the biggest gain was in maths.

What about the all-night revision session that many of you will be tempted by? I'm afraid the evidence is not on your side. After a night without any sleep, a person's ability to take in new information falls by about 40 per cent.

Some of you may be wondering about naps. A short nap of around twenty minutes can sharpen your concentration without making you feel worse afterwards. However, I'd advise against napping for longer than 30 minutes, unless you can fit in a full 90-minute cycle. Waking from deep sleep often causes what's called sleep inertia, a groggy, confused feeling that can last for up to an hour, and that rather defeats the purpose of a nap.
So, what practical advice does the research suggest? First, think about your bedroom. Many people keep it too warm, but it's best if it's dark, quiet and cool. Around 18 degrees is ideal.
And finally, a tip that may surprise you. Rather than leaving the hardest topics until the morning, review your most difficult material in the evening, shortly before bed.
To sum up, sleep isn't time wasted. It's when much of your learning is actually stored. Thank you for listening.

passages.title: Marlbury Town Council: changes to bus routes and fares from 4 January
paras: From Monday 4 January, Ridgeway Buses will introduce a number of changes to services in and around Marlbury. The changes follow a public survey in the autumn in which more than 2,000 residents took part, and the council would like to thank everyone who responded.
Route 12 (town centre to General Hospital): this popular service will now run every 15 minutes on weekdays, instead of every 20 minutes. Evening and weekend timetables are unchanged.

Route 7 (Fairfield to the railway station) will be withdrawn, because too few passengers were using it. Residents of the Fairfield estate will instead be served by Route 9, which will be extended to run through the estate before continuing to the station.
Route 31 (Dunmore Retail Park): the first bus of the day will now leave the bus station at 7.00 am instead of 8.30 am, to help people who work at the retail park. The last bus will remain at 9.15 pm.

Fares: the price of a single journey in the town zone will rise from 2 pounds 20 to 2 pounds 40, the first increase for three years. Day tickets will stay at £5.00 and weekly passes at £17.50. Holders of the Young Rider card, which is available to anyone aged 5 to 18, will continue to travel at half the adult fare. Passengers aged 65 and over who hold a council pass can travel free after 9.30 am on weekdays, and at any time at weekends.

Public meeting: if you would like to hear more or ask questions, please come to the Civic Hall on Thursday 10 December at 7.00 pm. Full timetables are available on the Ridgeway Buses website, or you can call the helpline on 0300 555 0142.

passages.title: Eastfield College: evening cooking classes for adults
paras: Whether you want to build confidence in the kitchen or simply try something new, our evening classes are taught by professional chefs in the college's fully equipped teaching kitchens. All courses begin in the week of 18 January. Enrolment closes on 9 January, and places are limited to 14 students in each class.

Knife Skills and Basic Techniques (Mondays, 6.30 to 8.30 pm, six weeks, 84 pounds). Designed for complete beginners, this course teaches you how to chop, slice and prepare ingredients safely, and how to cook a range of simple meals. No previous experience is needed.

World Street Food (Tuesdays, 7.00 to 9.00 pm, eight weeks, 112 pounds). Each week you will cook dishes from a different country, from Mexican tacos to Thai noodles, and finish the evening by tasting everything you have made. Some basic cooking skills are helpful.

Bread and Pastry Workshop (Wednesdays, 6.00 to 9.00 pm, five weeks, 95 pounds). This longer evening session covers loaves, pizza dough and pies, and you take home everything you bake. Students should already be confident with weighing and measuring.

Healthy Eating on a Budget (Thursdays, 6.30 to 8.30 pm, six weeks, 78 pounds). Learn how to plan meals, shop sensibly and make tasty dishes that cost very little. Basic skills such as boiling and frying are assumed. Every student receives a free recipe book containing all the course recipes.

Practical information. The cost of ingredients is included in all course fees. Students should bring an apron and a set of containers in which to take food home. Free evening parking is available in Car Park B, behind the sports hall. To enrol, telephone 01632 960 417 or visit the college website.

passages.title: Ostler & Reeve: annual leave and sickness absence, a guide for new employees
paras: Welcome to Ostler & Reeve. This guide explains how annual leave and sickness absence work during your first year with us. If anything is unclear, please ask your line manager or the Human Resources team.

Annual leave. Full-time employees receive 25 days of paid leave in each leave year, which runs from 1 April to 31 March, in addition to the usual public holidays. If you join part-way through the year, your entitlement is calculated according to the number of months you will work. Leave requests must be made through the staff portal, and you must give at least twice as many working days' notice as the number of days you want to take. For example, a request for five days off needs ten working days' notice. Your manager will reply within three working days. You may not take more than ten consecutive working days at one time without the approval of a director.

The office closes between Christmas Day and New Year's Day. Three of these days are treated as annual leave and are deducted from your entitlement. Up to five unused days may be carried forward to the next leave year, but they must be taken by the end of June or they will be lost.

Sickness absence. If you are too ill to work, you must telephone your line manager before 9.00 am on the first day of your absence. Emails and text messages are not acceptable, because a manager may not see them in time to arrange cover. For absences of up to seven calendar days, you complete a self-certification form on your return; after seven days, you need a fit note from your doctor. Whenever you have been off sick, you will have a short meeting with your manager on your first day back, to check that you are well enough to resume your duties and to discuss any support you need.

Sick pay. Once you have completed your six-month probationary period, you will receive full pay for up to ten days' sickness in any twelve-month period; after that, you receive statutory sick pay only. During probation you receive statutory sick pay from the first day. Medical or dental appointments should be arranged outside working hours wherever possible. If this is not possible, you should agree with your manager how the time will be made up. It will not be deducted from your annual leave.

passages.title: Writing effective work emails
paras: A  Subject lines. The subject line is the first thing your reader sees, and it often decides how quickly the message is opened. Avoid vague words such as 'Hello' or 'Question'. Instead, say exactly what the email is about, and if there is a deadline, include the date, for example 'Budget figures needed by 14 March'.

B  Greeting and tone. Match your style to the person you are writing to. 'Dear Ms Okoye' suits a first message to a customer, while 'Hi Sam' is usually fine for a close colleague. Whichever you choose, keep the language polite and avoid slang and jokes, which are easily misunderstood when the reader cannot see your face.

C  Structure. Busy people often read only the first few lines on a small screen, so put your main request or news at the beginning, and explain the background afterwards. Deal with one subject per email. If you have several points to make, use short paragraphs or a numbered list rather than a single long block of text.

D  Recipients and attachments. Send your message only to the people who need to act on it, and copy in others sparingly. Using 'reply all' by habit fills inboxes, and it can embarrass you if a private remark reaches the wrong person. If you mention an attachment, check that you have actually added it before you press send.

E  Emotion. Never write an email when you are angry. Strong feelings tend to show in the words you choose, and writing in capital letters is read as shouting. If a message has upset you, draft a reply, leave it for an hour, and then read it aloud before deciding whether to send it, or whether a phone call would be better.

F  Closing and follow-up. End with a clear next step, stating who should do what and by when. Read the whole message again to catch spelling mistakes, which can make a good message look careless. If you have had no reply after two working days, send a short, friendly reminder rather than assuming the message was ignored.

options: Up to five days can be carried forward until the end of June.
All unused days can be carried forward for three months.
Unused days are paid for at the end of the year.
Unused days are always lost on 31 March.
items.why: Up to five days may be carried forward but must be taken by the end of June.

items.q: How must employees report sickness on the first day?
options: by sending an email to their manager
by sending a text message
by completing a form on the staff portal
by telephoning their manager before 9.00 am
items.why: Employees must telephone the line manager before 9.00 am; emails and texts are not acceptable.

groups.instr: Do the following statements agree with the information in the guide? Choose TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.

items.q: Employees in their probationary period receive full pay for the first ten days of sickness.
items.why: Full sick pay starts only after probation; during probation employees receive statutory sick pay.

items.q: A doctor's note is needed if an absence lasts longer than seven calendar days.
items.why: Up to seven days needs self-certification; after seven days a fit note is required.

items.q: Employees are allowed to work from home when they have minor illnesses.
items.why: Working from home during illness is not mentioned in the guide.

items.q: Time taken off for medical appointments is deducted from annual leave.
items.why: The guide says the time will not be deducted from annual leave.

passages.title: The revival of the canals
paras: A  The great age of canal building lasted barely seventy years, from the 1760s to the 1830s, yet it transformed the way goods moved across the country. Before canals, heavy cargoes such as coal, pottery and grain had to travel along rutted roads that turned to mud in winter. A single horse walking along a towpath could pull a boat carrying thirty tonnes, a load that would have needed dozens of carts. The channels were dug almost entirely by hand by gangs of labourers known as navvies, who were paid by the amount of earth they shifted. To save money, many canals were built to a narrow width of just seven feet, and the long, slim boats that used them became known as narrowboats. Whole families lived aboard, cooking, sleeping and raising children in a cabin barely larger than a garden shed.

B  The railways changed everything. From the 1840s, trains could carry goods faster and, in many cases, more cheaply, and canal companies were forced to cut their tolls to keep their customers. Some canals were bought by railway owners who had little interest in keeping the water flowing, and maintenance was quietly neglected. Even so, the canals did not die at once. Motor engines, introduced on some boats in the early twentieth century, allowed a few firms to carry coal and building materials profitably for decades, and the last regular cargo on the Calder and Marsh Canal was not delivered until 1964. By then, however, lorries were taking most of the remaining trade, and the great majority of the network had fallen quiet.

C  By the 1950s, large stretches of waterway were in a sorry state. Weeds choked the channels, lock gates rotted and collapsed, and bridges were left unrepaired. Some canals were drained and filled in to make way for roads, car parks and housing. It was in this atmosphere that a retired schoolteacher called Margaret Hollis and a small group of friends founded the Waterways Rescue Society in 1946. Their first major campaign, in 1950, aimed to save the Wexley Navigation from closure, and it began with a protest in which more than sixty boats gathered over a single weekend, sounding their horns outside the offices of the authority that wished to shut it. The authority backed down, and the success persuaded many ordinary people that old canals might be worth saving.

D  Saving a canal is one thing; restoring it is another. Teams of volunteers, most of them with no previous experience, spent their weekends clearing mud, rebuilding walls and learning to lay bricks beside professional engineers. Progress was slow. The Calder and Marsh Canal, abandoned for over thirty years, took almost as long to bring back to life, with fourteen locks rebuilt before it reopened to boats in 2002. Funding was a constant struggle until lottery grants began to supplement the donations and the volunteers' unpaid labour, and the final bill came to some 28 million pounds. Local councils, at first sceptical, were won over when the figures showed how many visitors the reopened route attracted.

E  Today, the canals serve a very different purpose. The number of licensed boats has risen from around 4,000 in 1970 to more than 34,000, and while many are used for holidays, a growing number are permanent homes. Towpaths, once the preserve of horses, are now used by walkers, cyclists and anglers. Wildlife has returned as well: with the factories that once polluted the water long gone, otters and kingfishers can be seen in places where they had not been recorded for a century. Not every newcomer is welcome, however. A fast-spreading plant called floating pennywort has forced volunteer teams to spend many hours clearing it from the water each summer.

F  The revival has also changed the cities through which the canals pass. Derelict warehouses and wharves have been converted into apartments, offices and cafés, and property beside the water now sells for noticeably more than similar buildings a few streets away. Yet this success has brought tensions. Boat dwellers complain that moorings in popular areas have become scarce and expensive, and some long-standing residents feel that waterside developments are designed for wealthy newcomers rather than for the communities that grew up around the water. Meanwhile, the waterways' ageing structures, many of them built in the 1790s, need constant repair, and the charity responsible for them admits that it faces a maintenance bill it cannot meet from its own income.

G  Looking ahead, the canals may find new roles. Several experiments are under way to carry parcels into city centres on electric barges, taking lorries off crowded streets. Some buildings beside the water are already heated by pumps that draw warmth from the canal itself, and engineers believe the idea could be used much more widely. Perhaps the most important task, though, is to persuade younger people to take over from the ageing volunteers who did so much to rescue the waterways. As one veteran put it, the canals were saved by people who loved them, and they will survive only if a new generation learns to do the same.

groups.instr: The text has seven paragraphs, A-G. Which paragraph contains the following information? Choose the correct letter, A-G.

items.q: a plant that creates extra work for volunteers
items.why: Paragraph E mentions floating pennywort, which volunteers must clear each summer.

items.q: an explanation of how narrowboats got their name
items.why: Paragraph A says many canals were built narrow, so the boats became known as narrowboats.

items.q: the total cost of restoring one canal
items.why: Paragraph D gives the final bill for the Calder and Marsh Canal as some 28 million pounds.

items.q: an event that drew public attention to the threat to a canal
items.why: Paragraph C describes the protest of more than sixty boats outside the authority's offices.

groups.instr: Do the following statements agree with the information in the text? Choose TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.

items.q: Horses were used to pull boats along the canals.
items.why: Paragraph A says a single horse walking along a towpath could pull a thirty-tonne boat.

items.q: The Waterways Rescue Society had more than a thousand members by 1950.
items.why: The text gives the year the Society was founded and the date of its first campaign, but says nothing about how many members it had.

items.q: The Wexley Navigation was closed despite the protest.
items.why: The authority backed down, so it was not closed.

items.q: The volunteers on the Calder and Marsh Canal were all local residents.
items.why: Most had no previous experience, but where they lived is not mentioned.

items.q: Wildlife has returned to canals where it had not been seen for a century.
items.why: Paragraph E says otters and kingfishers can be seen where they had not been recorded for a century.

groups.instr: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

items.q: What does the writer say about property beside the canals?
options: It is mostly bought by boat owners.
It is cheaper than property elsewhere in cities.
It is worth more than similar buildings nearby.
It is rarely converted into cafés.
items.why: Paragraph F says waterside property sells for noticeably more than similar buildings a few streets away.

items.q: According to the writer, why are some boat dwellers unhappy?
options: It is hard to find affordable places to moor.
The towpaths are too crowded.
Wildlife damages their boats.
Licences have become too expensive.
items.why: Boat dwellers complain that moorings in popular areas have become scarce and expensive.

items.q: What problem does the charity responsible for the waterways face?
options: Its volunteers are leaving to work elsewhere.
Its structures were built badly.
Councils refuse to pay for repairs.
It cannot pay for all the repairs from its own income.
items.why: Paragraph F says it faces a maintenance bill it cannot meet from its own income; the structures are old, not badly built.

items.q: What does the writer suggest is most important for the future of the canals?
options: building more electric barges
attracting younger people to help care for them
extending the use of canal water for heating
persuading councils to fund restoration
items.why: The writer says the most important task is to persuade younger people to take over from the ageing volunteers.

task1.prompt:
You recently travelled by train and the journey was very poor. There were long delays, the train was overcrowded and passengers were given no information.

Write a letter to the train company. In your letter:
- describe what happened on your journey
- explain how the problems affected you
- say what you would like the company to do

Write at least 150 words. You do NOT need to write any addresses.

Begin your letter as follows:
Dear Sir or Madam,

task2.prompt:
More and more people now do their jobs from home instead of travelling to an office or workplace every day.

What are the advantages and disadvantages of this development?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
